author: Dan McAteer
text: Software engineering is the first knowledge work job solved by AI because the artifact produced by the SWE and the reasoning path to arrive at that artifact are one. Software engineering is the art of finding a logical law and then explicating that in code. Law, for example, is [not a logical artifact in the same way].
suggestedEngagement: Challenge with the enterprise agent deployment lens: 'Code generation is solved — but the harder problem is agent judgment: knowing when NOT to act, or when to escalate. That's not a logical artifact, and it's the thing that keeps enterprise deployments from going to prod.'

Extend the argument to other knowledge work: 'Does the same apply to data engineering? A pipeline or schema is also explicable as logical law. Or is there something unique to software that makes the artifact-reasoning unity so tight?'

Connect to the agent harness layer: 'If SWE is solved at the code level, the next layer is agents that understand organizational context — what to build and why. That's the harness problem, not the model problem.'

author: Lukasz Olejnik
text: A critical security flaw found by an Anthropic researcher (using AI) affects wolfSSL, a library used in products from VPN apps and home routers to automotive systems, power grid infrastructure, and military systems. CVE-2026-5194 could let a device or application accept a forged digital identity as genuine, trusting a malicious server, file, or connection it should have rejected. The flaw comes from missing digest-size and OID checks in signature verification, and Red Hat rates it CVSSv3 10.0 (max; remotely exploitable, no privileges required, no user interaction needed).
suggestedEngagement: Connect to the enterprise deployment angle: 'The scarier implication for enterprises is that agents using wolfSSL-based libraries for TLS could silently trust forged certificates from lateral-movement attacks. CVSSv3 10.0 in a dependency you may not even know you ship. What's your threat model for AI agents that inherit cryptographic trust from their host environment?'

Highlight the dual-use irony: 'Fascinating that the same AI pushing enterprises toward agent deployments is also the tool that found this flaw — and wolfSSL shows up in the very embedded infrastructure agents are starting to interact with. Glasswing may be the most underrated security initiative right now.'

Ask about scope awareness: 'The wolfSSL surface area is wild — VPNs, routers, automotive, military. What percentage of enterprises do you think know they ship wolfSSL transitively through their agent toolchains?'

recencyNote: Confirmed within 6-hour window — status ID indicates April 14, 2026 post

author: Lukasz Jachowicz
text: #Claude Code silently ignores user-configured security deny rules when a command contains more than 50 subcommands. #cybersecurity
suggestedEngagement: Add the enterprise harness angle: 'This is exactly why enterprise agent deployments need policy enforcement at the harness layer — not relying on client-side deny rules that can be bypassed by command complexity. The attack vector via CLAUDE.md in cloned repos makes this particularly dangerous for engineering orgs that allow agents to clone arbitrary repos.'

Ask about the broader pattern: 'Is this the first known case of a Claude Code security control being disabled by load rather than by explicit bypass? Curious whether the tree-sitter fix Anthropic already has in-repo got reviewed before the patch shipped.'

Challenge the risk framing: 'The CLAUDE.md supply chain vector is the most interesting part to me — it means any malicious open source repo can craft a compound command that disables deny rules on clone. How would you rate the real-world exploitability vs. the theoretical severity?'
